title: The Sunset Ramp
primary_metric: capital cost in dollars per MW/minute of evening ramp rate covered

options.A: The Solar Stack — 200 MW of solar plus a 4-hour, 200 MW battery
options.B: The Peaker Call — a new 120 MW natural-gas peaker plant

_ext: keys below are pipeline extensions, additive to SPEC §4
protagonist: Lena Marsh, resource-planning dispatcher, Cascade Grid Authority (fictional BA; real CAISO-anchored ramp data)
concept_sheet: C7 — The Sunset Ramp (brainstorm sheet, tier Advanced)

deliverables.text: A continuous model P(t) of net system load (MW) versus time (minutes) fit to the hourly evening net-load data points spanning the steepest part of the ramp, written as a polynomial in t, and its derivative dP/dt found using the power rule and reported as the instantaneous rate of change of net load with respect to time.

The equation of the tangent line to P(t) at the specific clock time of the steepest measured rise, with the tangent line's slope reported as the instantaneous ramp rate in MW per minute, plus an explicit justification that P(t) is differentiable at that point.

A ramp-response capability table: the battery's continuous full-power ramp-rate capability versus the gas peaker's minimum ramp rate after start, both converted to MW per minute, set against the instantaneous ramp rate from D2, with a covered / not covered determination for each option.

A dollars-of-capital-cost-per-MW-per-minute-of-ramp-rate-covered calculation for each option, using each option's total capital cost divided by the MW/minute of the D2 rate that option actually delivers (its own capability, capped at the D2 rate), with the percent margin between Option A's and Option B's cost-per-ramp-rate-covered shown explicitly.

balance.argument_a: The Solar Stack is the only option that covers the measured worst-instant ramp rate (137.5 MW/min) in full. A Hero who recommends B is knowingly leaving 87.5 MW/min of the evening's steepest measured minute uncovered by this resource alone. A's capital cost ($649,200,000) is higher, but it buys full coverage of the number the dilemma is actually about.
balance.argument_b: Per unit of ramp-rate actually delivered, The Peaker Call is 18.4% cheaper than The Solar Stack ($3,854,400 vs. $4,721,455 per MW/min) and delivers that rate all night, not just for the battery's bounded 4-hour discharge window. The 137.5 MW/min figure is itself a Modeling Assumption's peak instant (MA1), not a directly measured one, making full coverage of it an expensive hedge against an uncertain number.
balance.margin_basis: margin_pct = (costA - costB) / costA * 100, where costA = total capital cost of A ($649,200,000 = $300,400,000 solar + $348,800,000 battery) divided by the MW/min of the D2 rate (137.5) it delivers = $4,721,455/MW-min; costB = total capital cost of B ($192,720,000) divided by the MW/min it actually delivers, capped at its own 50 MW/min capability (below the 137.5 MW/min needed) = $3,854,400/MW-min. Option B wins the primary metric by 18.36%, but only by counting the smaller job (50 MW/min) it actually does, not the 137.5 MW/min the evening's measured worst instant demands -- Option A is the only option that fully covers that instant.

sensitivity_disclosure.justification: The D2 instantaneous rate (137.5 MW/min) is computed by quadratic interpolation through the three real-anchored hourly points of Appendix B, evaluated at the fitted window's edge -- not extrapolated past it. FACILITATOR.md's own sensitivity note already discloses that the peak rate could plausibly run 108 to 137.5+ MW/min depending on the curve's shape between anchors. A +-50% swing on this single anchor is a far larger perturbation than that documented range and both directions flip the recommendation to A -- a real instability in the fitted-curve modeling choice, not a data error.

Same interpolation method and same disclosed fragility as t60_net_load_mw above: this anchor is the other input to the quadratic fit that produces the D2 rate, evaluated within the fitted window per Appendix C (MA1). A +-50% swing here also flips the winner to A in both directions, consistent with the case's own acknowledged sensitivity of the fitted curve's shape.

RESEARCH_LOG.md P01: no manufacturer datasheet gives a precise full-power response time for this bid's specific battery chemistry/vendor; only a qualitative industry characterization ('near-instantaneous', 100-500ms) was found. The case's working 1-second figure is a documented conservative estimate from that public analogue, not a measured value -- flagged here per the Category-X exception. Note this dial never changes which option wins or the metric's value in this case: the battery's derived capability so vastly exceeds the required D2 rate at every flexed value that Option A's delivered rate stays pinned to the D2 rate itself, not to the battery's capability -- the flagged cap-breach is inherited unchanged from the base scenario's own margin, not created by flexing this dial.

modeling_assumptions.assumption: The five hourly net-system-load figures in Appendix B (16:00-20:00), used to fit the D1 model P(t)
modeling_assumptions.basis: A genuine attempt was made to source a real, timestamped, hourly-or-finer net-load or generation-by-fuel table for a specific real evening from EIA's Hourly Electric Grid Monitor, EIA's legacy Electricity Data Browser, CAISO's Today's Outlook/OASIS system, and CAISO's legacy Daily Renewables Watch archive; all four are genuine primary sources but none returned a fetchable, machine-readable table through the tools available this pass (see RESEARCH_LOG.md). The table instead reproduces exactly one real, dated, cited figure -- CAISO's own reported average net-load increase of 6.5 GW during the 6:00 p.m. hour (S5) -- placed between the 18:00 and 19:00 points, with the surrounding hours shaped to a realistic, smooth evening-ramp curve (flat afternoon, steepest at sunset, leveling off by 20:00).
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: The fitted model's peak instantaneous rate (D2, 137.5 MW/min) is sensitive to the exact curvature chosen between data points, not just the hourly totals -- a different quadratic matching the same 6,500 MW hourly total could plausibly return a peak rate anywhere from about 108 MW/min (the hourly average) up past 137.5 MW/min. This directly determines D3's covered/not-covered outcome for the peaker (its fixed 50 MW/min capability) and is flagged as prime Socratic material in FACILITATOR.md.

cohort_bands.note: 45-minute Socratic plan and anchor timings run as written in FACILITATOR.md. Anchor 1's stand-and-vote is a real split worth reading; the full deep-conflict thread and the backstop-battery twist both run at full length.

Anchors 2 and 3 combine into one pass ('what rate, over what instant'). Compress the Data Deep Dive to D2 and D4 only (skip walking D1's algebra step by step; hand out the fitted P(t) and focus discussion on what dP/dt means). Twist still drops at ~20 minutes. Total runtime ~30 min.

No show-of-hands vote at Anchor 1 -- the learner states an initial position instead. The guide argues the other side directly rather than cold-calling. Work D1-D4 together at the keyboard rather than as a room discussion; go straight from twist-recommit to Close.
